specAnchors.text: explain that gravitational force: • causes moons to orbit planets • causes the planets to orbit the Sun • causes artificial satellites to orbit the Earth • causes comets to orbit the Sun
describe the differences in the orbits of comets, moons and planets

primer.text: Gravity is the great choreographer: it bends moons around planets, planets around the Sun, satellites around the Earth and comets around the Sun. Planets ride near-circular paths in one plane and slow down with distance; comets loop on hugely stretched ellipses, sprinting past the Sun and drifting on the far leg.

modules.title: Gravity causes orbits
modules.opening: Orbital motion happens because of the gravitational attraction between two bodies. That force always points towards the centre of the larger body, and it holds the smaller body on its curved path: moons orbit planets, planets and comets orbit the Sun, and artificial satellites orbit the Earth.
keyPoints: Orbital motion results from gravitational attraction between two bodies.
Gravity's pull on the orbiter always points at the larger body's centre.
Gravity causes moons to orbit planets and planets to orbit the Sun.
Gravity also holds artificial satellites in orbit around the Earth and comets around the Sun.

low.restatement: Gravity aims at the big body's centre, so small bodies keep turning.
low.analogy: A ball on a string swung in a circle: the string tension (gravity) constantly pulls the ball inward, so it circles instead of flying off.
low.examPointer: List all four gravity-caused orbits — moons, planets, satellites, comets — when asked to 'explain that gravitational force causes'.

medium.restatement: Central attraction plus sideways motion equals an orbit: the pull supplies the constant inward turn.
medium.analogy: Whirling a bucket of water: the rope's inward tug is what stops the bucket sailing away in a straight line.
medium.examPointer: Name the larger body's centre as the pull's direction — that 'centre' wording is the mark.

modules.title: Planets and moons in orbit
modules.opening: Planets share habits: slightly elliptical orbits with the Sun near the centre, all in the same plane, all travelling the same direction — but they differ in radius, speed and period, with distant planets crawling and near planets racing. Moons orbit their planets in circular paths, and the closer the moon, the faster and shorter each orbit.
keyPoints: Planets orbit in slightly elliptical paths, in the same plane and the same direction.
Planets differ in orbital radius, speed and time taken to orbit.
The more distant the planet, the slower its travel and the longer its orbit.
Moons orbit planets in circular paths, faster when closer to the planet.

low.restatement: Planets: same plane, same direction, different radii — distance sets speed.
low.analogy: Runners on a track's outer lanes: the outside runners cover more ground at a jog while inside runners sprint their shorter laps.
low.examPointer: Split the answer into similarities (plane, direction) and differences (radius, speed, period) for full marks.

medium.restatement: Moon orbits are circular and distance-governed: close in means fast, far out means slow.
medium.analogy: Horses on a carousel: the inner horses finish each turn sooner than the outer ones.
medium.examPointer: Keep comet behaviour out of moon answers — circular and regular belong to moons and planets.

modules.title: Comet orbits
modules.opening: Comets break the planetary pattern: their orbits are highly elliptical or hyperbolic, they need not share the planets' plane or direction, and their speed swings wildly — increasing as they approach the Sun and decreasing as they recede.
keyPoints: Comet orbits are highly elliptical or hyperbolic.
A comet's speed changes a lot as its distance from the Sun changes.
Comets need not orbit in the planets' plane, and some travel the opposite direction.
Comets speed up as they approach the Sun and slow down as they move away.

low.restatement: Comets: stretched orbits, wild speed swings — fast near the Sun, slow far away.
low.analogy: A skateboarder in a half-pipe: fastest at the bottom (near the Sun), crawling at the rims (far away).
low.examPointer: 'Highly elliptical' is the phrase to quote; 'stretched circle' glosses it nicely in explanations.

medium.restatement: Speed and distance trade against each other along the comet's ellipse: closest approach is the fastest point.
medium.analogy: A bicycle descending a valley and climbing the far side: speed builds on the descent, drains on the climb.
medium.examPointer: Direction-of-travel questions: match 'approaching' with speeding up and 'receding' with slowing down.

glossary.definition: The attraction between bodies that steers orbiters around the larger body's centre.
A stretched-circle orbit; comets follow highly elliptical or hyperbolic paths.
How fast an orbiter moves; planets slow with distance, comets swing with theirs.
